caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Senegal's debt story was rewritten by scandal. From 17.5% of GDP in 2006 (post-HIPC), the ratio climbed steadily as the Sall government borrowed for infrastructure: the reported figure was 74.4% at end-2023. Then the September 2024 audit by the new Faye government revealed $11-13 billion in hidden debt, and the true ratio was revised to nearly 100% for 2023, reaching 132.4% in 2024, the series high, with 129.7% projected for 2025. The IMF suspended its $1.8 billion program over misreporting, and credit ratings collapsed into junk. A new $2.2 billion IMF program was agreed in principle in 2026. Senegal went in one audit from a manageable borrower to one of Africa's most indebted sovereigns.
inflation_management: Senegal's inflation is anchored by the CFA franc's peg to the euro and has been low for most of the period, with deflation in 2014 (-1.1%). The 2008 boom pushed it to 6.2% and the 2022 global shock to 9.7%, the series high, on food and energy prices. It fell back to 0.8% in 2024 and a projected 1.4% in 2025. The BCEAO's regional monetary policy has kept prices stable through the debt crisis, a striking contrast: monetary credibility survived even as fiscal credibility collapsed. But with debt at 130% of GDP, the peg's stability now depends on a fiscal adjustment the government has yet to deliver.

key_events.event: Macky Sall won the presidency; infrastructure borrowing began its long climb.
IMF $1.8 billion program approved (June 2023); Sangomar oil field neared production.
March 2024: Bassirou Diomaye Faye won the presidency on a reform platform.
September 2024: government audit revealed $11-13bn in hidden debt; true end-2023 debt was ~100% of GDP, not 74%; IMF suspended its program.
Sangomar oil produced first oil (June 2024); GTA gas neared production.
New $2.2 billion IMF program agreed in principle (2026); ratings remained deep in junk.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is a long, painful workout: oil and gas revenues (Sangomar, GTA) will help, but debt near 130% of GDP requires years of primary surpluses and the political will to sustain them. Upside is a successful IMF program restoring market access; downside is restructuring, which the government has resisted. Uncertainty is high: the hidden-debt revelation destroyed fiscal credibility, and rebuilding it will take longer than the numbers suggest.
